Released during the twilight of the studio-backed romantic comedy era, Robert Luketic’s *The Ugly Truth* (2009) presents a premise ripe with potential for sharp, modern battle-of-the-sexes humor. On paper, it has all the ingredients of a classic screwball comedy: an uptight, highly competent female lead, a brash and cynical male foil, and a high-stakes professional setting that forces them into reluctant collaboration. However, what could have been a clever, satirical dissection of contemporary romance instead collapses into a disappointing exercise in gender-cliché compliance. Ultimately, the film fails to deliver genuine humor or romantic satisfaction because it lazily surrenders to its male lead’s tired, sexist worldview rather than challenging or cleverly exploiting its premise.

The film introduces us to Abby Richter (Katherine Heigl), a neurotic, detail-obsessed TV producer struggling to rescue a failing Sacramento morning show. To boost the station's abysmal ratings, her boss hires Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), the boorish host of a local public-access show titled "The Ugly Truth." Mike’s philosophy on relationships is unapologetically crude and reductionist: men are driven purely by physical attraction and evolutionary impulse, while women’s expectations of love, intellect, and emotional intimacy are delusional fantasies. 

Desperate to save her job, Abby is forced to put up with Mike. When she meets her new neighbor, Colin (Eric Winter)—a handsome, polite, and seemingly perfect doctor—Mike strikes a bet with her. He promises to act as her personal dating coach, using his crass rules to help her land her dream man. If his advice works, Abby must accept his presence on the show; if it fails, he will resign.

This setup offers a ideal springboard for a Cyrano-esque narrative, or a dynamic update to classic screwball comedies like *His Girl Friday* or *It Happened One Night*. A truly clever comedy would have used this scenario to expose Mike’s chauvinism as a fragile defense mechanism, contrasting his cynical rules with the messy, unpredictable reality of actual human connection. It would have allowed Abby to maintain her dignity and intellect while proving that relationships cannot be reduced to shock-jock tricks.

Instead, *The Ugly Truth* makes a fatal creative error: it repeatedly proves Mike right. 

To win Colin over, Abby is instructed to abandon her personality, alter her physical appearance, repress her opinions, and act like a submissive, airheaded fantasy. The narrative rewards her for this deceit. Colin falls for the fake, sanitized version of Abby, validating Mike’s claim that men only care about long hair, push-up bras, and feigned docility. Rather than subverting Mike’s vulgar philosophy, the script turns him into a crude prophet. The humor suffers immensely as a result; instead of witty banter born from two equal minds clashing, the jokes rely on the audience accepting lazy stereotypes—that all women are uptight, nagging shrews, and all men are simplistic, sex-obsessed Neanderthals.

Even the film's inevitable romantic turn feels completely unearned. As Abby and Mike begin to develop feelings for each other, the story attempts to convince us that Mike has soft-hearted depth beneath his boorish exterior. But because his misogynistic worldview has been vindicated by the plot at every turn, his character never undergoes any meaningful growth. He doesn't learn to respect women; Abby simply lowers her standards to meet him on his level. When Abby inevitably chooses Mike over Colin, it does not feel like a victory for true, messy love—it feels like a surrender to the very cynicism the movie claimed to critique.

By prioritizing cheap, regressive gags over genuine character development and sharp writing, *The Ugly Truth* squanders its talented cast and vibrant premise. The real "ugly truth" of the film isn't a secret insight into male psychology, but rather a depressing reflection of a studio system that chose lazy, outdated gender tropes over smart, lasting comedy.

The red light atop Camera 3 glowed like a drop of fresh paint, signaling to millions of viewers worldwide that Katherine was live. Behind her, the iconic, gleaming red-and-white CNN logo served as the backdrop for what was supposed to be the defining moment of her journalism career. 

At thirty-four, Katherine had spent a decade chasing stories through mud, rain, and political firefights to earn a seat at the main anchor desk in Atlanta. Tonight was a prime-time breaking news special, a high-stakes broadcast covering a volatile international summit. She had spent seventy-two hours straight prepping, memorizing names, policy details, and historical contexts. She felt ready.

Then, the unthinkable happened.

Ninety seconds into the broadcast, the primary teleprompter glitched, freezing on a single, scrambled sentence. Katherine’s heart hammered against her ribs, but as a seasoned professional, she didn't panic. She gracefully transitioned to her paper notes, relying on her memory to bridge the gap. 

She turned to her live guest, a notoriously stern former Ambassador, to ask a crucial opening question regarding a delicate treaty. But under the suffocating heat of the studio lights and the pressure of the ticking clock, Katherine’s exhaustion caught up with her. The names spun in her head.

Instead of referring to the key geopolitical ally by their correct country, she confidently conflated two entirely different nations, accidentally referencing a fictional country from a popular thriller novel she had been reading to fall asleep the night before.

The Ambassador stared at her, his eyebrows raising in utter disbelief. "Katherine," he said, his voice echoing with cold condescension, "I don't know what continent you think we're discussing, or if CNN has started covering make-believe geography, but that is patently absurd."

A heavy, suffocating silence filled the studio. Katherine’s blood ran cold. She tried to correct herself, but in her sudden panic, she stumbled over her words, stammering aimlessly while trying to find the right page in her notes. The live camera zoomed in slightly, capturing her wide-eyed panic, the bead of sweat tracing down her temple, and the complete collapse of her composure.

In her earpiece, the executive producer’s voice barked in a mix of fury and mercy: *"Cut to commercial! Cut to commercial now!"*

The screen went black, transitioning to a detergent advertisement, but the damage was already done. 

The immediate aftermath was a blur of quiet, crushing humiliation. Within minutes, the clip had escaped the television screen and infested the internet. Social media erupted. The phrase "CNN Katherine" was trending globally, accompanied by thousands of memes, reaction GIFs, and sharp commentary mocking her mistake. 

When she stepped off the set, the studio was painfully quiet. Colleagues averted their eyes, offering awkward, pitying smiles—the kind reserved for people who had just suffered a tragic, irreversible accident. 

Katherine walked back to her dressing room, closed the door, and sank into the couch. The shame burned in her chest like liquid fire. She had spent her entire adult life building a reputation for intelligence, precision, and poise, and in five agonizing seconds, she felt it had all been erased.

She looked at her reflection in the lit vanity mirror. Her makeup was still pristine, her hair perfectly styled, but behind her eyes was a deep, humbling ache. 

Later that night, sitting in the quiet of her apartment with her phone turned off, the initial wave of agony began to settle into something else. The humiliation was immense, yes, but as she stared out at the city skyline, a quiet truth emerged: the worst had happened. Her nightmare—failing on a global stage—had come true, and she was still breathing. 

News cycles move fast. By tomorrow, the world would find a new distraction. Katherine knew the path back to credibility would be steep and unforgiving, but as she wiped away a solitary tear, she resolved that this singular, mortifying moment on CNN would not be the final line of her story.

**CNN Entertainment**

### Movie Review: ‘The Ugly Truth’ exposes Hollywood’s most cynical romantic comedy instincts

**By Tom Vance, CNN**

**(CNN) —** There is a moment early in Robert Luketic’s *The Ugly Truth* where Gerard Butler’s character, a shock-jock relationship guru named Mike Chadway, boldly declares that men are incapable of loving women for their minds, hearts, or personalities. Men, he insists, are purely driven by primal, visual lust. 

It is meant to be a moment of provocative truth-telling. Instead, it serves as an unintended thesis statement for the film itself: a movie thoroughly convinced that its audience is too stupid, too superficial, and too desperate to demand anything resembling real human emotion.

The "ugly truth" of the title isn't a revelation about modern dating; it’s the realization of how utterly bankrupt the studio romantic comedy had become by 2009.

The plot pairs Katherine Heigl—then at the peak of her post-*Grey’s Anatomy* reign as Hollywood’s go-to strung-out blonde—with Gerard Butler, fresh off *300* and apparently eager to bring the same caveman bravado to a morning news program. Heigl plays Abby Barns, a control-freak TV producer in Sacramento whose show is dying in the ratings. Enter Mike (Butler), a local cable host whose segment, "The Ugly Truth," features him spewing misanthropic, baseline misogyny under the guise of "telling it like it is."

To save her ratings, Abby is forced to work with Mike. To save her nonexistent love life, she agrees to let him coach her in winning over her handsome, bland neighbor, Colin (Eric Winter).

What follows is a tedious battle of the sexes that feels less like a comedy and more like a sentence served in a corporate focus group. 

Mike’s advice to Abby is as reductive as it is offensive: don’t laugh at your own jokes, don’t talk about your work, get hair extensions, and wear push-up bras. In short, erase your personality. The film’s script—penned by a committee of three female writers, bafflingly enough—expects us to root for Abby as she systematically hollows herself out to attract a man who doesn't actually exist outside of a Sears catalog.

Heigl, a talented comedic actress with sharp timing, is trapped in a loop of her own making. Playing yet another neurotic, emotionally stunted career woman who just needs a coarse man to unbutton her top collar, she is given nothing to work with except slapstick embarrassment. (Yes, there is an infamous scene involving vibrating underwear at a business dinner—a sequence so profoundly unfunny it makes one long for the subtle grace of a pie in the face.)

Butler, meanwhile, leans heavily into a brand of aggressive, smirking charisma that quickly curdles into pure unpleasantness. Mike isn't a lovable rogue or a charming cynic; he is a workplace harassment lawsuit waiting to happen. The film asks us to believe that beneath his aggressively crude exterior beats the heart of a sensitive soul who just needs the right woman to tame him. But there is zero chemistry between Heigl and Butler. Watching them bicker feels less like *it-happened-one-night* spark and more like two actors shouting over the noise of a failing script.

When the inevitable third-act turn arrives—where the cynic and the romantic realize they are meant for each other—it feels entirely unearned. They don't fall in love because of any shared growth or genuine connection; they fall in love because the genre’s algorithm dictates that the runtime has hit 90 minutes.

*The Ugly Truth* tries to position itself as an edgy, R-rated reality check for hopeless romantics. But behind its dirty jokes and coarse language lies a deeply conservative, deeply lazy movie that insults both men and women in equal measure. 

If this is what passes for romance, the truth isn't just ugly—it's downright depressing.

***

**Verdict:** 1.5 out of 4 stars

*The Ugly Truth is rated R for crude and sexual content, and language.*

**Review: ‘The Ugly Truth’ Proves the Only Thing Uglier Than Modern Romance is This Script**

**By CNN Entertainment Critic**

If you were sitting in a movie theater in 2009, you might remember feeling a distinct, creeping sense of dread about the state of American cinema. Cinema didn't die with a bang; it died with the romantic comedy assembly line. And sitting squarely at the top of that scrap heap is Robert Luketic’s *The Ugly Truth*, a film that takes the sophisticated, razor-sharp genre of screwball comedy, drags it into an alley, and beats it to death with a rolled-up copy of *Maxim* magazine.

The premise—if we dare call it that—stars Katherine Heigl as Abby, a neurotic, uptight TV producer who (gasp!) cares about her job and reads books. Naturally, this makes her deeply unlovable. Enter Gerard Butler as Mike Chadway, a cable-access shock jock who dresses like a mid-level nightclub promoter and sounds like a Scottish caveman who just discovered body spray. Mike’s entire brand is telling women "the truth": men are visual creatures who only care about sex, and women are over-thinking harpies who need to shut up and buy push-up bras. 

In a classic setup that would make Howard Hawks roll over in his grave, the studio forces Abby to hire Mike to boost ratings. Naturally, sparks fly—if by "sparks" you mean the dull, grinding noise of two actors realizing their agents lied to them.

The film desperately wants to be a modern *His Girl Friday* or *It Happened One Night*. But true screwball comedy requires two essential ingredients: lightning-fast banter driven by intellectual equals, and a subversion of societal norms. *The Ugly Truth* has neither. Its idea of "wit" is Gerard Butler aggressively explaining male physiology using hot dogs, while Heigl makes appalled faces that suggest she just smelled burnt toast. 

Instead of subverting gender dynamics, the film enthusiastically embraces the kind of Neanderthal pseudo-science you’d expect from a 19-year-old pickup artist on Reddit. The overarching thesis of the movie is that for a woman to find love, she must completely surrender her personality, put on a slinky dress, pretend to care about sports, and never, under any circumstances, speak her mind. Mike teaches Abby how to land her "dream guy"—a blandly handsome neighbor played by Eric Winter—by instructing her to act like a lobotomized swimsuit model. 

And what is the film’s idea of high-stakes, sophisticated comedy? A scene where Abby accidentally wears remote-controlled vibrating underwear to a critical corporate dinner, only for the remote to fall into the hands of a small boy at a nearby table. Cue Heigl writhing in a restaurant booth, faking an orgasm over a plate of salmon. It’s a moment designed to evoke Meg Ryan in *When Harry Met Sally*, but it achieves all the warmth and grace of an infomercial for a failing adult novelty shop. 

The most terrifying part of *The Ugly Truth* isn’t the lazy dick jokes or the relentless misogyny—it’s the inevitable third-act twist. After an hour and a half of Mike treating women like disposable chew toys, we are supposed to swoon when Abby realizes *he* is the one for her. Why? Because underneath that coarse, woman-hating exterior lies a man who is... well, still a coarse woman-hater, but now he’s sad about it. 

Heigl, who once had the charisma to carry a scene, is reduced to a twitchy cartoon of female anxiety. Butler, meanwhile, smirks his way through the runtime, radiating the charm of a guy who cuts you off in traffic and flips you the bird. Together, they have the romantic chemistry of a root canal.

In the end, *The Ugly Truth* delivers on its title, though not in the way the filmmakers intended. The truth is ugly indeed: Hollywood once thought audiences were dumb enough to believe that verbal abuse plus a makeover equals true love. Skip this one, and rewatch a Cary Grant movie instead. Your brain cells—and your faith in humanity—will thank you.

**Rating:** 1/5 stars (and the 1 star is only because the credits eventually rolled).

### **The Premise**
Abby Richter (Katherine Heigl) is a neurotic, checklist-obsessed Sacramento TV producer whose morning news show is suffering from abysmal ratings. She is also chronically single because her expectations for men are unrealistically high. Enter Mike Chadway (Gerard Butler), a cynical, shock-jock relationship "expert" whose local cable show, *The Ugly Truth*, preaches that men are simple creatures driven entirely by sex and visual attraction. 

When Abby’s station hires Mike to boost ratings, the two immediately clash. However, when Abby meets her seemingly perfect neighbor, a handsome doctor named Colin (Eric Winter), she agrees to a deal: Mike will act as her romance coach to help her land the doctor. If his crude advice works, she promises to work peaceably with him. But as Mike’s tactics start working, Abby and Mike begin to realize that opposites might actually attract.

---

### **What Works: The Star Power and Chemistry**
The absolute strongest element of *The Ugly Truth* is the undeniable charismatic chemistry between Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler. 

* **Katherine Heigl** was at the peak of her romantic-comedy reign here, and she excels at physical comedy and playing the uptight, control-freak archetype. She leans into the absurdity of her character with total commitment—most notably in a memorable, outrageous scene involving vibrating underwear at a business dinner.
* **Gerard Butler** brings a charismatic, rogueish energy to Mike Chadway. Even when his character says deeply offensive and chauvinistic things, Butler’s natural charm keeps the character from being entirely unlikable. 
* **The Banter:** When Heigl and Butler are sparring verbally, the movie is genuinely fun. They trade quick, snappy insults that give the film a lively, high-energy momentum.

---

### **What Doesn't Work: Clichés and Outdated Tropes**
Where *The Ugly Truth* stumbles is in its script, which relies heavily on tired, offensive gender stereotypes. 

* **Reductive Gender Politics:** The movie frames relationships through an extremely narrow lens: *All women want fairy-tale romance and are overly nagging; all men are mindless apes who only care about physical appearance and sex.* While it’s meant to be a lighthearted "battle of the sexes," the cynicism can occasionally feel lazy rather than funny.
* **Predictability:** From the very first 10 minutes, you know exactly how the movie will end. It follows the standard romantic-comedy formula beat-for-beat without adding any unique twists to the genre.
* **The Message:** The underlying message—that Abby must completely alter her personality, suppress her intelligence, and dress differently just to get a man to like her—feels cheap, even if the movie tries to backtrack on this idea in the third act.

---

### **The Verdict**
*The Ugly Truth* is the quintessential late-2000s R-rated romantic comedy. It wants to be edgy and crude (think *Sex and the City* meets *When Harry Met Sally*), but deep down, it’s a remarkably soft, highly formulaic studio picture. 

If you go in expecting a sharp, progressive piece of cinema, you will likely be disappointed and annoyed by the gender clichés. However, if you are looking for a **guilty-pleasure movie night** with charismatic leads, laugh-out-loud slapstick moments, and easy-to-digest banter, Heigl and Butler make it worth a casual watch.

**Best Suited For:** Fans of Katherine Heigl’s rom-com era (*27 Dresses*, *Knocked Up*), lovers of enemies-to-lovers tropes, and anyone looking for a raunchy, brain-off romantic comedy.

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN.com/SHOWBIZ/MOVIES**

**(CNN)** — If you thought the Hollywood romantic comedy was entirely dead, *The Ugly Truth* arrives to prove it is merely alive, kicking, and swearing like a sailor. 

Directed by Robert Luketic (*Legally Blonde*), this battle-of-the-sexes comedy takes the worn-out boy-meets-girl formula and douses it in a heavy splash of R-rated cynicism and raunchy vulgarity. While it hardly reinvents the wheel, the film relies heavily on the undeniable, oil-and-water chemistry of stars Katherine Heigl and Gerard Butler to keep the machine running.

Heigl plays Abby Richter, a hopelessly neurotic, control-freak TV producer for a struggling Sacramento morning news show. Abby’s love life is a wasteland of disastrous dates, primarily because she relies on a literal checklist of qualifications for her ideal man. 

Enter Mike Chadway (Butler), a boorish, hyper-masculine cable access host whose show, "The Ugly Truth," preaches a ruthless gospel to women: men are simple creatures who care only about physical attraction and sex, not your personality or career ambitions.

When Abby’s station manager hires Mike to boost ratings, the two immediately clash. But when Abby falls for her swoon-worthy, seemingly perfect new neighbor, Colin (Eric Winter), she strikes a deal with her crude new co-worker. If Mike can coach her into landing the handsome doctor using his predatory dating manual, she will work with him peacefully. If he fails, he quits.

What follows is a brisk series of comedic set pieces where Abby acts as Mike’s puppet, shedding her uptight exterior to play the ultimate male fantasy. 

The film finds its biggest laughs when it throws Abby into wildly uncomfortable situations. During a pivotal scene at a local baseball game, Mike coaches Abby through an earpiece from the concourse, instructing her to laugh at bad jokes, toss her hair, and tell the guy he’s "so big"—leading to a sequence of absurd, cringe-inducing public flirting in the middle of the bleachers.

Even more memorable is a chaotic dinner scene at a high-end restaurant. Dressed to impress Colin, Abby makes the mistake of wearing a pair of remote-controlled vibrating underwear that Mike purchased for her. Naturally, the remote ends up in the hands of a young boy at a neighboring table, leading to a loud, public, and hilarious breakdown of Abby's composure that feels like an homage to Meg Ryan's famous *When Harry Met Sally...* scene, albeit with a modern, filthy upgrade.

Predictably, as Abby begins to transform and Colin takes the bait, Mike begins to realize that he might be falling for his own creation—and Abby discovers that the cynical shock-jock has a heart under his coarse exterior. 

*The Ugly Truth* doesn't break any ground narrative-wise. You can spot the romantic twist coming from the opening credits. Furthermore, some of the script's gender politics feel retrograded, wrapping up progressive themes in decidedly regressive tropes. 

Yet, Heigl proves once again that she is one of the most reliable slapstick comedic actresses of her generation, playing the straight-woman to Butler’s brash Scottish charm. Butler, radiating effortless roguish charisma, seems to be having the time of his life shedding his *300* action-hero skin for R-rated laughs.

**The Verdict:**
If you can stomach the vulgarity and overlook the formulaic plot, *The Ugly Truth* offers enough genuine laughs and starry spark to make for an enjoyable date night—even if the truth it delivers is pretty predictable.

***

**FILM REVIEW INFO:**

* **Title:** The Ugly Truth
* **Studio:** Columbia Pictures / Relativity Media
* **Director:** Robert Luketic
* **Cast:** Katherine Heigl, Gerard Butler, Eric Winter, Cheryl Hines, John Michael Higgins
* **MPAA Rating:** Rated R for crude and sexual content throughout, and language.
* **Running Time:** 96 minutes
* **Release Date:** July 24, 2009

**Film Review: *Corner Office Romance* (2008)**
**Rating:** ★☆☆☆☆  
**By:** [Your Name]  
**Date:** October 14, 2008  

If the late 2000s has taught us anything about Hollywood’s vision of the modern woman, it’s that a high-paying job, a sharp blazer, and an opinion are the tragic symptoms of a terminal psychological defect. Nowhere is this regressive, nauseating thesis more proudly displayed than in *Corner Office Romance*, a movie so steeped in toxic double standards that it functions less as a romantic comedy and more as a 90-minute disciplinary hearing for a woman daring to have a career.

The premise is as formulaic as it gets: Kate (played with heroic effort by an actress who deserves a better agent) is a ruthless, highly competent marketing executive in Manhattan. We know she is cold and unfulfilled because she wears her hair in a tight bun, carries a BlackBerry, and—heaven forbid—expects her subordinates to do their jobs. Enter Brody (a smirking, stubbled man-child), a co-worker who spends his days playing desk-golf, turning in assignments late, and making borderline-actionable sexual comments in the breakroom. 

In a sane world, Kate would have Brody escorted out of the building by security before the first act breaks. But this is a late-2000s studio rom-com, which means Brody isn’t a liability—he’s her *savior*. He is here to teach her how to "loosen up," which apparently involves sabotaging her presentation, taking her to a dirty dive bar against her will, and forcefully pulling the hairpin out of her bun so her hair tumbles down in full, male-gaze-approved glory.

The double standard at the heart of *Corner Office Romance* isn't just annoying; it is downright offensive. 

When Kate demands excellence, she is branded a "hysterical, frozen shrew." When Brody acts like an irresponsible, patronizing frat boy, the movie plays whimsical accordion music and frames him as a charming free spirit. Kate is required to go through a painful, humiliating arc of self-flagellation—she must realize that her ambition was just a mask for loneliness, apologize for being "bossy," and ultimately abandon a career-defining promotion in the third act to prove she has a heart. 

And what does Brody have to do to win her over? Absolutely nothing. He doesn't grow. He doesn't apologize for his unprofessionalism. He simply turns up at her apartment building in the rain, makes a speech about how "imperfect" she is, and gets rewarded with a woman who has systematically dismantled her own self-respect just to meet him at his level. 

To see how far the genre has fallen, one only needs to look back at the gold standards. Consider *When Harry Met Sally...* (1989). Nora Ephron’s masterpiece worked precisely because Harry and Sally were allowed to be equally flawed, equally neurotic, and equally human. Sally Albright was high-maintenance and particular, yes, but the film never punished her for it, nor did it demand she change into a completely different person to be worthy of love. Harry was held accountable for his cynicism just as Sally was challenged on her rigidity. It was a duel of equals. 

Even further back, the great screwball comedies understood that a strong woman made the romance *better*. Katharine Hepburn didn't spend the 1930s and 40s going toe-to-toe with Spencer Tracy or Cary Grant just so her 21st-century successors could be told to put down the laptop and bake a pie. When Hepburn played an uncompromising, whip-smart woman in *Adam’s Rib* or *Woman of the Year*, she was allowed to keep her intellect. The men had to level *up* to meet her; she wasn't forced to lobotomize herself to make a man feel secure. 

If Katharine Hepburn were alive to watch *Corner Office Romance*, she would likely throw her shoe at the screen. 

*Corner Office Romance* is a depressing relic of an era obsessed with putting successful women back in their place, wrapped up in a cheap, glossy pink bow. It tells young women that competence is unsexy, that boundaries are a flaw, and that the ultimate romantic fantasy is settling for a man who resents your success. Save your money, skip this cinematic hate-crime against women, and rewatch *Bringing Up Baby* instead.
